items.title: Phoebe Jacobs and Jackie Harris interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 21, 2006
items.q: He wasn’t cultured, like Denzel Washington or one of those cats.

ctx.x: I would say that you can’t be emphatic enough about that. I have often thought having Satch the day that they called me to come to the office that Louis Armstrong passed, and I sat in a room where the head of every country, the head of every country, the presidents, the governors, the outpouring for this man’s death was so outstanding that no matter how I measured him in his being vital to the world, I could never estimate how great it was. And of course the longer he lives the more I know how great he is because…

stopped. Thank God it’s never stopped. Every day of my life I get at least a minimum of two inquiries for the use of something of Louis Armstrong — his face, his voice, a tape — that’s a minimum. And it comes from all over the world. But the interesting thing about this whole deal of people loving Louis is I try to analyze what is it. He wasn’t handsome by standards of handsomness, like he wasn’t a Harry Belafonte or a Sidney Poitier. He wasn’t cultured, like Denzel Washington or one of those cats. But he had…
When I listen to some of the Hot Five and Hot Seven, it sounds so new to me for that time. It’s just unbelievable the exuberance that came out of his instrument. Indescribable.
